oils.name: Grapeseed Oil
oils.chefVerdict: Gold Standard: High linoleic acid provides resilient, non-brittle cross-linking that expands and contracts with thermal cycling without micro-cracking.
oils.cautions: Buy pure expeller-pressed or refined grapeseed oil without additives or silicone anti-foaming agents.

oils.name: Canola / Rapeseed Oil
oils.chefVerdict: Universal Workhorse: Readily available, affordable, excellent balance of oleic and linoleic acids yielding durable, flexible polymer coats.
oils.cautions: Ensure thin wipe-down before baking to avoid localized sticky pooling in pan crevices.

oils.name: Soybean Oil (Standard Commercial Vegetable Oil)
oils.chefVerdict: Factory Baseline: Primary oil utilized by Lodge Manufacturing for foundry pre-seasoning. Excellent substrate adhesion and cost efficiency.
oils.cautions: Requires 475°F oven temperature to ensure full catalytic cross-linking.

oils.name: Crisco / Hydrogenated Vegetable Shortening
oils.chefVerdict: Heritage Favorite: Solid room-temperature state prevents running, allowing effortless ultra-thin microscopic film buffing before entering the oven.
oils.cautions: Use standard neutral vegetable shortening; avoid butter-flavored variants containing diacetyl and moisture.

oils.name: Flaxseed / 100% Raw Linseed Oil
oils.chefVerdict: Brittle Glass Paradox: Extremely high alpha-linolenic acid creates a rock-hard cross-linked polymer, but internal crystalline tension makes it brittle. Commonly flakes and peels after 3-6 months under thermal shock or metal spatulas.
oils.cautions: Do NOT use boiled linseed oil from hardware stores (contains heavy metal toxic drying catalysts like cobalt and manganese). Must be organic food-grade flaxseed oil, refrigerated.

oils.name: Refined Avocado Oil
oils.chefVerdict: Under-Polymerization Risk: Exceptional for high-heat pan searing, but suboptimal for oven seasoning. Its 520°F smoke point requires extreme 550°F oven cycles to cross-link oleic acid; standard baking leaves a tacky, gummy semi-liquid film.
oils.cautions: Reserve avocado oil for searing steaks in already well-seasoned iron, not for building baseline seasoning.

oils.name: Extra Virgin Olive Oil (EVOO)
oils.chefVerdict: Scorched Polyphenols: Free fatty acids, particulate matter, and chlorophyll scorch into acrolein and carbonized char rather than smooth polymers, creating a mottled, dull, easily degraded coating.
oils.cautions: Never use unrefined extra virgin olive oil for base seasoning. High-heat degradation releases noxious acrolein vapors.

oils.name: Rendered Lard / Beef Tallow (Pure)
oils.chefVerdict: Heritage Traditional: Widely used historically before the advent of liquid seed oils. Forms a soft, hydrophobic protective grease layer, but lacks double bonds to form dense polymer matrices.
oils.cautions: If stored in humid kitchen pantries without frequent use, unpolymerized animal fats undergo hydrolytic rancidity and turn sour.

oils.name: Bacon Grease / Pan Drippings
oils.chefVerdict: Corrosion & Char Hazard: Popular internet folklore, but scientifically hazardous for base seasoning. Contains dissolved table salt (NaCl), sodium nitrite, and burnt microscopic protein debris that pit iron and char into sticky grit.
oils.cautions: Salt ions catalyze galvanic micro-pitting in raw iron, and burnt animal meat particulate accelerates rancidity and off-odors.

oils.name: Virgin / Refined Coconut Oil
oils.chefVerdict: Non-Polymerizing: Contains 90%+ saturated medium-chain fatty acids (lauric, myristic). Lacks carbon-carbon double bonds required for cross-linking. Liquefies at 76°F and washes off immediately with warm water.
oils.cautions: Cannot form a polymer coating. Do not attempt seasoning with coconut oil.

cookwareSubstrates.name: Modern Sand-Cast Iron (Lodge, Victoria, Cuisinel)
cookwareSubstrates.description: Molten iron poured into green-sand molds leaves a characteristic pebbled texture. High surface micro-voids provide immense mechanical anchoring for polymerized oils, making seasoning extremely resilient against flaking.

cookwareSubstrates.name: Vintage / CNC-Milled Smooth Cast Iron (Griswold, Wagner Ware, Field, Smithey)
cookwareSubstrates.description: Machined or stone-ground surface leaves a satin-smooth finish. Offers superior initial non-stick release for eggs, but lower mechanical tooth means thick seasoning layers will flake off if oil is applied too heavily.

cookwareSubstrates.name: Carbon Steel Skillet (de Buyer, Matfer Bourgeat, Darto)
cookwareSubstrates.description: Composed of 99% iron and ~1% carbon stamped from cold-rolled steel. Heats and cools 3x faster than cast iron. Benefits immensely from high-heat stovetop blueing (forming Fe3O4 magnetite) prior to applying oil.

cookwareSubstrates.name: Enameled Cast Iron (Le Creuset, Staub, Lodge Color)
cookwareSubstrates.description: Coated in fused vitreous glass enamel. DO NOT SEASON. Oil baked onto enamel creates a stubborn, burnt polymer varnish that degrades cookware release. Clean solely with warm water, mild soap, or baking soda.

acidicFoods.name: Lemon Juice / Vinegar Reduction (Pan Sauces)
acidicFoods.notes: Directly strips young or thin polymer bonds within 5-10 minutes. Imparts strong metallic iron taste and causes gray discoloration.

acidicFoods.name: Simmered Tomato Marinara / Ragù
acidicFoods.notes: Simmering longer than 30 minutes chelate iron ions through polymer micro-fissures. Leaches 15-30mg of bioavailable non-heme iron per serving, turning sauce dark brownish-black.

acidicFoods.name: Red Wine Braise / Beef Bourguignon
acidicFoods.notes: Wine tannins and tartaric acid attack both the seasoning and the underlying metallic iron. Braises exceeding 1 hour require Dutch ovens with vitreous enamel.

acidicFoods.name: Seared Steaks, Burgers & Pork Chops
acidicFoods.notes: High fat and high heat actively reinforce and build the seasoning polymer layer via continuous in-situ lipid cross-linking.

acidicFoods.name: Fried Eggs, Cornbread & Dutch Babies
acidicFoods.notes: Neutral to slightly alkaline foods preserve and polish the smooth polymer surface without chemical disruption.

failureModes.name: Sticky, Tacky, Gummy Surface (Oil Pooling)
failureModes.cause: Too much oil applied before heating, or oven temperature below the oil's critical polymerization threshold.
failureModes.chemistry: Liquid triglycerides partially oxidized into viscous oligomers without completing full radical cross-linking into a solid insoluble polymer.
failureModes.remedy: Bake the skillet upside down at 450°F (232°C) for 1 hour to complete polymerization. If gummy pool is thick, scrub with coarse kosher salt and a dry towel or strip with lye.

failureModes.name: Flaking & Peeling Black Seasoning Specks
failureModes.cause: Seasoning with brittle drying oils (flaxseed), applying coats too thickly, or sudden thermal shock (quenching hot pan in cold water).
failureModes.chemistry: Internal shear strain exceeds polymer tensile strength; lack of ductile accommodation causes crystalline delamination from iron substrate.
failureModes.remedy: Scrub away all loose flakes with stainless steel chainmail scrubber. Apply micro-thin layers of grapeseed or canola oil and bake at 450°F.

failureModes.name: Orange Flash Rust (Hydrated Iron Oxide Fe2O3)
failureModes.cause: Moisture exposure after stripping or washing without immediate dry-heating and oil sealing.
failureModes.chemistry: Elemental iron (Fe) reacts with dissolved oxygen and water to form loose hematite/rust (Fe2O3 · nH2O). Oil applied over flash rust will not adhere.
failureModes.remedy: Wipe away rust with a paper towel soaked in distilled white vinegar (5% acetic acid). Immediately dry on a hot stovetop, apply micro-thin oil, and heat until smoking.

failureModes.name: Burnt Food Carbon Crust (Falsely Mistaken for Seasoning)
failureModes.cause: Cooking at excessive heat (>600°F) or failure to clean caramelized food residue and sugar drippings.
failureModes.chemistry: Pyrolyzed biomass forming soft, porous amorphous carbon. Unlike cross-linked lipid polymers, carbon crust traps bacteria, flakes into food, and promotes sticking.
failureModes.remedy: Scrub thoroughly with chainmail and mild dish soap. True polymerized seasoning is chemically bound to the iron and is unaffected by modern dish soap (which contains no lye).

flakingSeasoningIngestion.mechanism: Polymerized fatty acid chains (polyolefin-like plastics) are chemically inert and cannot be broken down by human gastric acid or pancreatic lipases. Ingested flakes pass harmlessly through the GI tract.
flakingSeasoningIngestion.dailyIntakeSafety: Safe (Cosmetic culinary defect rather than toxicological hazard)

dietaryIronLeaching.clinicalImpact: Beneficial dietary supplement for iron-deficiency anemia patients. However, individuals with Hereditary Hemochromatosis (HFE gene mutation causing systemic iron overload) must avoid cooking acidic sauces in unlined cast iron.

freeRadicalPeroxides.safetySummary: Normal oven seasoning at 450°F creates stable covalent polymers. However, heating unseasoned oil above its smoke point on stovetops without food ventilation releases volatile acrolein, an eye and respiratory irritant.
